profile.longBio:
I am a PhD student in Organizational Behavior at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University.
My research asks how experiences within and beyond work shape well-being, engagement, and leadership. My work spans recovery activities and work engagement, parenting and leadership development, social perceptions of leaders, career growth, and responses to stress. I approach these questions through evidence synthesis, field research, and quantitative analysis.
Beyond my own research, I founded [BWJ OB Pluto](https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/BjEi-r94QIzPFTiwJjfrXA), an academic column that shares organizational behavior research and reflections on academic life. I value making research accessible and building a community in which researchers can learn from one another.
profile.interestDetails:
Recovery & Well-being | How do activities outside work relate to recovery and engagement at work? My ongoing work uses theoretical synthesis and meta-analysis to examine these connections. [Related working paper](#record-work-1)
Leadership & Life Experiences | How do family experiences and parenting practices relate to leadership? My published work examines benevolent leadership and adolescent leader emergence. [Parenting and leadership](#record-pub-3)
Social Perception & Career Development | How do perceptions of leaders and leader–employee relationships shape leadership emergence and career growth? This line connects work on perceived cuteness, career calling, and career crafting. [Career calling study](#record-77d1b65e-a9c1-4a08-9bad-7698bf7a6a0a)
Research Methods & Evidence Synthesis | I am interested in bringing together systematic reviews, meta-analysis, longitudinal data, and computational approaches to understand psychological and organizational processes. [Machine-learning study](#record-pub-4)

entries.title: Being a Parent Helps Being a Benevolent Leader: A Mixed-Method Approach
entries.authors: Liu, Z., Liang, Z., Wang, C., & Bian, W.
entries.summary: Leadership development can draw on experiences beyond the workplace. This study examines how positive parenting experiences relate to benevolent leadership through the resources parents bring to their work roles.
entries.researchQuestion: How can positive parenting experiences translate into more benevolent behavior toward employees?
entries.researchApproach: Study 1 analyzed written accounts from 13 parent-role leaders and interviews with 16 others. Study 2 used a two-wave survey of 364 leaders who were also parents in mainland China, with approximately two months between waves.
entries.researchFindings: Positive parenting experiences were linked to benevolent leadership through perspective taking. The association with perspective taking, and the indirect association with benevolent leadership, were stronger when co-parenting quality was higher.
entries.topics: Benevolent leadership; Parenting experiences; Perspective taking; Co-parenting; Work–family enrichment

entries.title: Leadership Blossoms in Parental Warmth: Positive Parenting Practices Shape Adolescent Leader Emergence via Intrapersonal and Interpersonal Mechanisms
entries.authors: Liu, Z., Bian, W., & Bian, Y.
entries.summary: Leadership can begin to develop long before a formal work role. This study investigates the family as a setting for adolescent leader emergence, focusing on parental warmth and encouragement of independence.
entries.researchQuestion: How is parental warmth related to adolescent leader emergence, and what personal and interpersonal processes help explain this association?
entries.researchApproach: A mixed-method design combines multi-source data from 1,255 adolescents and their parents, teachers, and peers with in-depth interviews involving 32 adolescents.
entries.researchFindings: Parental warmth was positively associated with leader emergence through two pathways: self-esteem and leader self-efficacy, and empathy and prosocial behavior. Encouragement of independence strengthened the positive association. Interviews added examples of supportive parenting practices.
entries.topics: Adolescent leadership; Parental warmth; Leader emergence; Self-efficacy; Empathy; Independence

entries.imageCaption: Figure 1. Mixed-methods research model of parental warmth and adolescent leader emergence.

entries.title: Using Machine Learning to Explore the Predictors of Life Satisfaction Trajectories in Older Adults
entries.authors: Chen, H., Zhang, X., & Bian, W.*
entries.summary: Life satisfaction in later adulthood follows different paths over time. This study combines trajectory analysis and machine learning to identify those paths and the factors that help distinguish them.
entries.researchQuestion: Which trajectories of life satisfaction occur among older adults in China, and which characteristics predict membership in those trajectories?
entries.researchApproach: Using four CHARLS waves (2011, 2013, 2015, and 2018), the study followed 2,600 adults aged 60 or older. Latent class growth and growth mixture models identified life-satisfaction trajectories; five machine-learning classifiers predicted trajectory membership.
entries.researchFindings: Four trajectories were identified. Random forest performed particularly well in predicting trajectory membership. Happiness, loneliness, body mass index, and self-rated health were important predictors; these are predictive associations rather than evidence of causal effects.
entries.topics: Life satisfaction; Older adults; Longitudinal research; Machine learning; Trajectory analysis

entries.title: How Does Leader Career Calling Stimulate Employee Career Growth? The Role of Career Crafting and Supervisor–Subordinate Guanxi
entries.authors: Ni, X., Zhu, X., Bian, W., Li, J., Pan, C., & Pan, C.
entries.summary: A leader’s sense of calling may matter for employees’ careers as well as the leader’s own. This study examines career crafting as a link between leader career calling and employee career growth.
entries.researchQuestion: How does leader career calling relate to employee career growth, and when does supervisor–subordinate guanxi strengthen this process?
entries.researchApproach: Study 1 was a scenario experiment with 208 participants. Study 2 surveyed 490 full-time employees in a Chinese electrical-appliance enterprise in Hangzhou to test the full model of career crafting, career growth, and supervisor–subordinate guanxi.
entries.researchFindings: Career crafting mediated the relationship between leader career calling and employee career growth. Higher-quality supervisor–subordinate guanxi strengthened the calling–crafting relationship and the associated indirect relationship with career growth.
entries.topics: Career calling; Career crafting; Career growth; Supervisor–subordinate guanxi

entries.imageCaption: Figure 1. Research model of leader career calling, career crafting, and career growth.

entries.title: Autonomic Nervous System Response Patterns of Test-Anxious Individuals to Evaluative Stress
entries.authors: Bian, W., Zhang, X., & Dong, Y.
entries.summary: Evaluative situations can produce similar feelings of arousal but different physiological responses. This study examines how people with high versus low test anxiety respond to an interview-based stressor.
entries.researchQuestion: Do high- and low-test-anxious individuals show different autonomic and emotional responses to evaluative stress?
entries.researchApproach: A standardized interview task induced evaluative stress in 48 participants with high test anxiety and 49 with low test anxiety. Heart-rate variability and subjective emotion were measured across baseline, stress, and recovery phases.
entries.researchFindings: Both groups reported increased arousal and showed increased low-frequency HRV. Only the high-test-anxiety group showed significant decreases in pleasantness, high-frequency HRV, and RMSSD during stress, indicating a different pattern of autonomic regulation.
entries.topics: Test anxiety; Evaluative stress; Heart-rate variability; Autonomic regulation; Emotion
